opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important to distinguish between an agent that's been built for one task and an agent that genuinely learns. When we had systems like TD-Gammon, or later AlphaZero for chess and Go, or the DQN work on Atari, those were real accomplishments. They showed that reinforcement learning, learning from experience, from reward, could reach superhuman levels. But each of those was, in a sense, a separate project. You set up the environment, you train the agent, and you get a specialist.

What we don't yet have is an agent that carries what it learned in one setting into another. If you train on one Atari game and then move to the next, the typical result is that it doesn't transfer well. Often it's worse than that: you get catastrophic interference, where learning the new thing destroys what it knew before. That tells us our methods for generalization aren't good yet. We have function approximators that generalize, but nothing in our algorithms really causes them to generalize *well*, in a way that's useful across tasks. When it works, it's usually because people have sculpted the representations by hand, or tuned the setup until it does.

So the way I think about it is that the goal isn't a chess agent or an Atari agent. The goal is an agent that lives in a world, a continual learner, that's always learning from its stream of experience, and for which chess or an Atari game is just one part of its life. It should come to each new situation with what it has already learned, and it should learn the new thing without forgetting the old. That's what animals do, it's what people do, and it's really the big open problem. We need continual learning and good generalization, and I'd say we're still at an early stage with both.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames chess and Atari as parts of one agent’s life in a world and says it should bring prior learning to each new situation, conveying them as different situations within that world.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that chess and Atari were never really the point. They were test beds. What we're actually after is an agent that can go into any environment, with no special knowledge handed to it, and learn to do well there from experience. The chess programs and the Atari systems were steps toward that, and I think they were good steps, but they are also a little misleading about what the real problem is.

Take Atari. The thing that was interesting about DQN was not that it played Breakout. It was that the same system, with the same learning algorithm and the same architecture, could be dropped into dozens of different games and learn each one. That's the generality we care about. But notice what's still missing. It learned each game separately. It didn't carry anything from one game to the next. A person who learns Pong and then sits down at Breakout brings an understanding of balls and paddles and walls. The Atari agents brought nothing. They started over.

And chess, or Go, is in some ways even further from what I'd call the real problem. In those cases you're given the model of the world. You know the rules. You can simulate ahead perfectly. That's a huge gift, and it's not one the world gives you. In the actual world you have to learn the model, and your model is always going to be wrong in some ways, and you have to plan with a model you know is imperfect. That is the hard thing. AlphaZero is wonderful, but it sidesteps that.

So when I think about handling different tasks, I'm less interested in the list of tasks and more interested in whether the agent is doing the same fundamental things in each case. Is it perceiving, is it predicting what will happen, is it learning from the consequences of its actions, is it building knowledge that it can use again? If it's doing those things, then the variety of tasks follows. If instead each new task needs a new trick from the designer, then we haven't really built an agent, we've built a tool, and the intelligence is still in us.

I'd also say the right notion of generality here is continual. One agent, one long life, many problems arriving over time, and it keeps getting better. Our current systems mostly learn once and then freeze. That is a very odd thing to call intelligence. The animals we're modeling ourselves on don't do that. So the goal, for me, is not an agent that can be trained to play chess and also trained to play Atari. It's an agent that can be put in the world and learn whatever it needs to, and keep learning.

r001.rationale: The response describes chess and Atari as separate games or environments to learn in; it does not characterize them as different states within a single world.

astra-6.text:
Well, you have to distinguish between using the same learning algorithm on different tasks and having one agent that can do all those tasks. Those are different claims. You might take an algorithm, train it on chess, and train another instance on an Atari game. That shows some generality in the algorithm, but it doesn’t necessarily show that anything learned in chess helps with Atari.

The reinforcement learning perspective is that these problems share a structure: an agent takes actions, receives observations and rewards, and learns to act so as to get more reward over time. You don’t have to build the rules of chess into the learning algorithm. But that common formulation doesn’t make learning every task equally easy.

The more interesting question is whether an agent can keep learning, carrying what it has learned into new situations. Can it develop representations and ways of behaving that are useful beyond the particular task on which it acquired them? That’s a much stronger kind of generality than starting over with the same algorithm each time.

r001.rationale: The response describes chess and Atari as separate tasks trained in separate instances; it does not characterize them as different states encountered within one world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between using the same learning algorithm for different tasks and having one agent that can learn many tasks. You might take a reinforcement learning algorithm, train it on chess, and then start over and train it on an Atari game. That shows some generality in the algorithm, but it doesn’t show that the agent can carry knowledge from one task to another.

The more interesting goal is an agent that keeps learning. It encounters a new task, brings what it has already learned, and improves through interaction. Reinforcement learning gives us a common way to describe these problems: the agent acts, receives observations and rewards, and learns to get more reward. But having that common formulation doesn’t by itself solve the problem of transfer. You still have to learn representations and ways of acting that are useful beyond the particular situation in which you learned them.

r001.rationale: The response treats chess and Atari as separate tasks and discusses training or transferring between them. It does not describe them as different states encountered within a single world.
